'''''Rotheca myricoides''''' or '''Butterfly Clerodendrum,'''  '''Butterfly Bush,''' and ('''butterfly bush''' – also a name for ''[[Buddleja]]'' species) is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Lamiaceae]].<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | ''Rotheca myricoides'' | 447341 | access-date = 2009-04-13}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=LLC |first=Top Tropicals |title=Rotheca myricoides, Clerodendrum ugandense, Butterfly Clerodendrum, Blue Butterfly Bush, Blue Glory Bower, Blue Wings |url=https://toptropicals.com/catalog/uid/clerodendrum_ugandense.htm |access-date=2024-12-07 |website=TopTropicals.com - rare plants for home and garden |language=en}}</ref> It is native to tropical eastern [[Africa]] and widely cultivated elsewhere.<ref name=GRIN/> In cultivation, it is frequently known by one of its [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]], such as ''Clerodendrum myricoides''.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Clerodendrum myricoides'' 'Ugandense'  |work=Plant Finder |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=a496 |access-date=2015-07-24 }}</ref>

The [[cultivar]] 'Ugandense' is an untidy [[evergreen]] shrub growing to {{convert|4|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall and {{convert|2.5|m|ft|abbr=on}} broad, with oval leaves and masses of pale-violet blue butterfly-like flowers in summer and autumn. Each flower has a darker blue lower petal. With a minimum temperature of {{convert|10|C|F|abbr=on}}, this plant can only be grown under glass in [[temperate climate|temperate]] zones. The altitude range for this species is 900–1680 m.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Steane |first1=D. A. |last2=Mabberley |first2=D. J. |date=1998 |title=Rotheca (Lamiaceae) Revived |journal=Novon |volume=8 |issue=2 |page=204 |doi=10.2307/3391997 |jstor=3391997 |issn=1055-3177}}</ref> The plant has won the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/353598/Rotheca-myricoides-Ugandense/Details | title = ''Rotheca myricoides'' 'Ugandense' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 17 February 2021}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
''Rotheca myricoides'' is native to mountains from [[Eritrea]] to [[South Africa]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=Rotheca myricoides (Hochst.) Steane & Mabb. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science|url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:1002729-1|access-date=2022-12-04|website=Plants of the World Online|language=en}}</ref> It is native to [[Angola]], [[Botswana]], [[Burundi]], [[Caprivi Strip]], [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]], [[Djibouti]], [[Eswatini]], [[Eritrea]], [[Ethiopia]], [[Kenya]], [[KwaZulu-Natal]], [[Malawi]], [[Mozambique]], [[Namibia]], [[Northern Provinces]], [[Rwanda]], [[Somalia]], [[Sudan]], [[Tanzania]], [[Uganda]], [[Zambia]], and [[Zimbabwe]].<ref name=":2"/> It was introduced to [[Trinidad and Tobago|Trinidad-Tobago]], [[Australia]], and [[Brazil]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Rotheca myricoides (Hochst.) Steane & Mabb.|url=https://www.gbif.org/species/7307157|access-date=2022-12-04|website=www.gbif.org|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2"/>

== Habitat ==
This species may be found in rocky places, streams and edges of the evergreen forest.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=Flora of Botswana: Species information: Rotheca myricoides |url=https://www.botswanaflora.com/speciesdata/species.php?species_id=149090 |access-date=2022-12-06 |website=www.botswanaflora.com}}</ref> The shrub thrives in frost free climates, tolerating full sun to part shade, but preferring part shade and moist, well-drained soils rich in organic matter.<ref name=":13"/> In colder climates, 'Ugandese' is often grown in containers as it cannot stand temperatires below 10 °C (50 °F).<ref name=":13">{{Cite web |title=Rotheca myricoides 'Ugandense' (Blue Butterfly Bush, Blue Glory Bower, Butterfly bush) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/rotheca-myricoides-ugandense/ |access-date=2024-12-07 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> If temeperatures fall below -3.9 °C (25 °F) the plant may die, but rejuvenates from its roots in spring.<ref name=":13" />

== Etymology ==
The [[genus]] name, [[Rotheca]], seemingly comes from the Malaysian words "cheriga", which means small, and "thekku", which means teak.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Rotheca myricoides 'Ugandense' - Plant Finder|url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=a496|access-date=2022-12-04|website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref> The species [[epithet]] comes from the French word "myriades", which means ten thousand, and a Latinization of the Greek "oides", which means to see.<ref name=":1" /> Some say that the species epithet came about because it resembles another species in Myrica, so the name refers to the leaf shape.<ref name=":12" />

'Ugandense' is a [[cultivar]] of this species which shows purplish-blue flowers with flashy stamens.<ref name=":1" /> It was originally named ''Clerodendrum myricoides'' 'Ugandense', but a 1998 study led to its current status as ''Rotheca myricoides'' 'Ugandense".<ref name=":1" />

== Morphology ==

=== Flowers ===
The flowers are arranged in dichasial [[cymes]] and are sometimes arranged in short-pedunculate [[panicle]]s.<ref name=":2"/><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=Rotheca myricoides (Hochst.) Steane & Mabb.|url=http://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000298156;jsessionid=BC2DD73EEC85683B8CFACBAACA87E6BC#citation2|access-date=2022-12-04|website=www.worldfloraonline.org|language=en}}</ref> The [[stamen]]s and [[Style (botany)|styles]] are long-exserted and curve upwards.<ref name=":3" /> The [[Corolla (plant)|corolla]] is asymmetrical in the bud and they have a mid-lobe dark blue or violet blue, while the lateral lobes are pale blue or mauve.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> The [[Sepal|calyx]] is bud-shaped with a 5mm long tube, and the lobes are rounded to triangular.<ref name=":2" />

There is lots of variation in the flower colour. It can be green and blue or mauve, white and blue, or blue to mauve.<ref name=":5"/>

=== Fruits ===
The fruits of this species are 5-6 by 8–10 mm in dimension and are mostly deeply four-lobed.<ref name=":2" /> To attract birds the plant produces small, black, drupe-like fruits when pollinated.

=== Leaves ===
The leaf outline is mostly [[Ovate (leaf)|ovate]] to rhomboid.<ref name=":5">{{cite book |chapter=Labiatae (Lamiaceae) – Hausa potato family |date=1988 |title=Flowering Plants in West Africa |pages=258–263 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/cbo9780511551505.032 |isbn=978-0-521-26192-0 }}</ref> The outline can sometimes be [[Elliptic leaf|elliptic]] or [[Glossary of leaf morphology|obovate]].<ref name=":5" /> The leaf margin is dentate or deeply lobed.<ref name=":5" /> The indumentum of the leaves can vary. There is often a hairy upper surface, and the lower surface can be sparsely to densely hairy. It has been described as feeling velvety.<ref name=":5" /> When the leaves are crushed, there is an unpleasant scent.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Verdcourt |first=B |title=Flora of Tropical East Africa-Verbenaceae |year=1992}}</ref> This may be due to the pelate hairs or pelate glands on the leaves.<ref name=":6" /> The leaves are opposite whorls of 3–4.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Thulin |first=Mats |date=1999 |title=A New Combination for a Grewia (Tiliaceae) from Somalia |journal=Kew Bulletin |volume=54 |issue=4 |pages=1007–1008 |doi=10.2307/4111185 |jstor=4111185 |issn=0075-5974}}</ref> The petiole is 0–24 mm long.<ref name=":0" />

=== Branches ===
The young branches are normally angular, pale greyish-whitish and with white [[lenticel]]s. They are hairy, mostly at the growth points. The arrangement of the main branches are normally opposite. There are prominent leaf scars on the branches as well.<ref name=":6" /> The branches can be four-angled and brownish-red towards the apex. The lateral branches are short, leafy and flowering.<ref name=":0" />

== Medicinal uses ==

=== Traditional ===
''Rotheca myricoides'' is used in traditional medicine to manage [[diabetes]] in the lower eastern part of [[Kenya]]. This area is populated mostly by the [[Kamba people|Kamba]] community.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Keter |first1=Lucia K. |last2=Mutiso |first2=Patrick C. |date=January 2012 |title=Ethnobotanical studies of medicinal plants used by Traditional Health Practitioners in the management of diabetes in Lower Eastern Province, Kenya |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=139 |issue=1 |pages=74–80 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2011.10.014 |pmid=22020309 |issn=0378-8741}}</ref> They take this medicine daily by boiling and consuming the leaves.<ref name=":4" /> This species is also used to treat [[epilepsy]], [[arthritis]], [[Typhoid fever|typhoid]], cough, eye problems, [[tonsillitis]], [[rheumatism]], [[Gonorrhea|gonorrhoea]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Moshi |first1=Mainen J. |last2=Otieno |first2=Donald F. |last3=Weisheit |first3=Anke |date=2012-04-04 |title=Ethnomedicine of the Kagera Region, north western Tanzania. Part 3: plants used in traditional medicine in Kikuku village, Muleba District |journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine |volume=8 |issue=1 |page=14 |doi=10.1186/1746-4269-8-14 |issn=1746-4269 |pmc=3349493 |pmid=22472473 |doi-access=free }}</ref> cancer,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tadesse |first1=Tesfaye Yimer |last2=Zeleke |first2=Mulugeta Molla |last3=Dagnew |first3=Samuel Berihun |date=September 2022 |title=Review of Ethnobotanical and Ethnopharmacological Evidence of Some Ethiopian Medicinal Plants Traditionally Used for Peptic Ulcer Disease Treatment |journal=Clinical and Experimental Gastroenterology |volume= 15 |pages=171–187 |doi=10.2147/ceg.s384395 |pmid=36186925 |pmc=9517940 |s2cid=252507350 |issn=1178-7023|doi-access=free }}</ref> [[malaria]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mukungu |first1=Nillian |last2=Abuga |first2=Kennedy |last3=Okalebo |first3=Faith |last4=Ingwela |first4=Raphael |last5=Mwangi |first5=Julius |date=December 2016 |title=Medicinal plants used for management of malaria among the Luhya community of Kakamega East sub-County, Kenya |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=194 |pages=98–107 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2016.08.050 |pmid=27586821 |pmc=5176009 |s2cid=18111784 |issn=0378-8741|doi-access=free }}</ref> [[dysmenorrhea]], [[Sterility (physiology)|sterility]], and [[impotence]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sawadogo |first1=W.R. |last2=Maciuk |first2=A. |last3=Banzouzi |first3=J.T. |last4=Champy |first4=P. |last5=Figadere |first5=B. |last6=Guissou |first6=I.P. |last7=Nacoulma |first7=O.G. |date=March 2012 |title=Mutagenic effect, antioxidant and anticancer activities of six medicinal plants from Burkina Faso |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/14786419.2010.534737 |journal=Natural Product Research |language=en |volume=26 |issue=6 |pages=575–579 |doi=10.1080/14786419.2010.534737 |pmid=21809951 |s2cid=205837271 |issn=1478-6419|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In traditional medicine, European and African cultures used the bark of the species in its powdered form, and a teaspoon is used to treat snakebites.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last=Miller |first=James S. |date=1997-09-01 |title=Zulu Medicinal Plants: An Inventory By A. Hutchings with A. H. Scott, G. Lewis, and A. B. Cunningham (University of Zululand). University of Natal Press, Pietermaritzburg. 1996. xiv + 450 pp. 21 × 29.5 cm. $133.00. ISBN 0-86980-893-1. |journal=Journal of Natural Products |volume=60 |issue=9 |page=955 |doi=10.1021/np970084y |issn=0163-3864}}</ref> The [[Maasai people|Masai]] used the root bark for [[East Coast fever]] in cattle and diarrhea in their calves.<ref name=":7" /> The [[Haya people|Haya]] and Shambala used ''Rotheca myricoides'' for [[Dysmenorrhea|dysmenorrhoea]] and cough, [[furunculosis]] and swellings that are associated with [[Debility (medical)|debility]].<ref name=":7" /> In various African communities, the root of the plant is also used for chest pain, colds, gum bleeding  indigestion, headaches, and bathing people with convulsions.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fang |first=Xiaoai |last2=Zhang |first2=Siyi |date=2021-09-02 |title=The complete chloroplast genome sequence of Rotheca myricoides (Hochst.) Steane & Mabb., a traditional medicinal plant |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/23802359.2021.1966340 |journal=Mitochondrial DNA Part B |language=en |volume=6 |issue=9 |pages=2699–2700 |doi=10.1080/23802359.2021.1966340 |issn=2380-2359|pmc=8382008 }}</ref> In West Africa, the plant is used for [[analgesic]] and [[antipyretic]] purposes.

In Asian countries, this species has been brewed as a tea to relieve swelling and pain.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Matsabisa |first1=Motlalepula Gilbert |chapter=African traditional herbal medicine: Addressing standardization and quality control challenges for product development |date=2022 |title=Evidence-Based Validation of Herbal Medicine |pages=561–586 |publisher=Elsevier |last2=Tripathy |first2=Satyajit |last3=Dassarma |first3=Barsha |last4=Chabalala |first4=Hlupheka P. |last5=Mukherjee |first5=Pulok Kumar|doi=10.1016/b978-0-323-85542-6.00027-5 |isbn=978-0-323-85542-6 }}</ref>

=== Recent studies ===
A 2019 study looked at freeze-dried extracts of the ''Rotheca myricoides'' and found that they possess significant [[Antihyperglycemic|anti-hyperglycemic]] and antidyslipidemic effects on a [[type 2 diabetes]] rat model. The antidyslipidemic effects included decreased total plasma cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, serum triglyceride and increased HDL-cholesterol.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last1=Chege |first1=Boniface Mwangi |last2=Waweru |first2=Mwangi Peter |last3=Frederick |first3=Bukachi |last4=Nyaga |first4=Nelly Murugi |date=November 2019 |title=The freeze-dried extracts of Rotheca myricoides (Hochst.) Steane & Mabb possess hypoglycemic, hypolipidemic and hypoinsulinemic on type 2 diabetes rat model |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=244 |article-number=112077 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2019.112077 |pmid=31369832 |s2cid=199380202 |issn=0378-8741}}[[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]]  Text was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/  Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License].</ref> The freeze-dried extracts also lowered the serum [[Uric acid|uric]] levels and [[Hepatic triglyceride lipase|hepatic triglycerides]] and [[hepatic]] weight.<ref name=":9" /> This study confirms the effectiveness of the traditional medicine to manage diabetes in Kenya. The mechanism for the antidiabetic effects is due to the modulation of PPAR-γ.<ref name=":8" />

A 2008 study found that ''Rotheca myricoides'' had [[antimutagen]]ic properties.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last1=Verschaeve |first1=L. |last2=Van Staden |first2=J. |date=October 2008 |title=Mutagenic and antimutagenic properties of extracts from South African traditional medicinal plants |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=119 |issue=3 |pages=575–587 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2008.06.007 |pmid=18602977 |issn=0378-8741}}[[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]]  Text was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/  Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License].</ref> The leaf extract of the species and [[DCMU|DCM]] and [[Meoh|MeOH]] extracts shows clear anti-mutagenicity. The antimutagenic properties were seen even at low doses of 0.05 mg/L.<ref name=":9" />

''Rotheca myricoides'' is one ingredient (along with four African medicinal plants: ''[[Clerodendrum glabrum]]'' E. Mey., ''Lamiaceae'', ''[[Gladiolus dalenii]]'' van Geel, and ''[[Senna occidentalis]]'' (L.) Link) in a new [[COVID-19]] therapeutic candidate called PHELA.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last1=Matsabisa |first1=M. G. |last2=Alexandre |first2=K. |last3=Ibeji |first3=Collins U. |last4=Tripathy |first4=S. |last5=Erukainure |first5=Ochuko L. |last6=Malatji |first6=K. |last7=Chauke |first7=S. |last8=Okole |first8=B. |last9=Chabalala |first9=H. P. |date=2022-06-19 |title=In vitro study on efficacy of PHELA, an African traditional drug against SARS-CoV-2 |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=10305 |doi=10.1038/s41598-022-13599-y |pmid=35718800 |pmc=9207029 |bibcode=2022NatSR..1210305M |s2cid=249868349 |issn=2045-2322|doi-access=free }} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]]  Text was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/  Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License].</ref> In vitro testing found that PHELA inhibited >90% of [[SARS-CoV-2]] and [[SARS-CoV-1|SARS-CoV]] infection at concentration levels of 0.005 mg/mL to 0.03 mg/mL.<ref name=":10" />  They also found that PHELA had very strong binding energy interactions with SARS-CoV-2 proteins.<ref name=":10" />

== Ecology ==
The ''Rotheca myricoides'' interacts with several other species.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |title=search |url=https://www.globalbioticinteractions.org/?interactionType=interactsWith&targetTaxon=Rotheca%20myricoides |access-date=2022-12-06 |website=www.globalbioticinteractions.org}}</ref> ''Pseumenes depressus'', the [[Asian hornet]], and Xylocopa ruficeps all visit the ''Rotheca myricoides''. ''Xylocopa phalothorax'', ''Xylocopa tranquebarorum'', and ''[[Xylocopa nasalis]]'' eat the ''Rotheca myricoides.''<ref name=":11" /> The plant plays a significant role in its native ecosystems by supporting pollinators like butterflie and bees. Its long corolla tubes are adapted to attract specific pollinators with long proboscises for effective pollen transfer. The plant provides food to birds that consume its drupes, helping in seed dispersal.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rotheca myricoides – PLANTBOOK |url=https://www.plantbook.co.za/rotheca-myricoides/#:~:text=Family:%20Lamiaceae%20(Mint%20family),delightful%20blue%20flowers%20in%20summer. |access-date=2024-12-07 |website=www.plantbook.co.za}}</ref>

The status on the Red List of South African plants is at "Least Concern" as assessed on 2005/06/30, as it was not highlighted as a potential taxa for conservation concern.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Threatened Species Programme {{!}} SANBI Red List of South African Plants |url=http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=7980-5 |access-date=2022-12-06 |website=redlist.sanbi.org}}</ref>
